the lacustrine stratal architecture of the Lamayurudelta is characterized by a marked contrast between clastic-rich and carbonate-rich facies, which is attributed to the semi-arid alpine setting of the former Lake Lamayuru.

The Lamayuru lake was in existence at least by 35,000 and possibly persisted until 1000 years ago; it was created by a 200 m thick landslide; its sediments include thin turbidites, laminated muds and abundant, diverse, biologically dominated shallow water carbonates; and the alpine semiarid environment favors diversified, spacialy restricted carbonate sedimentation with sporadic clastic inputs.

the sedimentary response of a semiarid alpine lake to the episodic input of clastics from its alpine catchment and to the biological productivity of the lake itself.
the sedimentary processes and facies associations of a lacustrine succession in the semiaridal alpine environment of the Ladakh Himalaya.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Lamayuru lake was a shallow-water, semi-arid, carbonate-rich, lacustrine basin, which was intermittently fed by alpine debris flows and permafrost meltwater.
the lacustrine stratas in Ladakh typified many of the carbonate rich Pleistocene alpin lakes found in the semi-arid environment of the Northern Himalaya.

the alpine lakes in the semi-arid environment of the northwestern Himalaya were characterized by a depositional regime that favored carbonate-dominated shallow-water, bioturbated, laminated, and bedded strata punctuated by clastic lenses representing debris flow and periglational input.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Lamayuru lake was a carbonate-rich alpine lake that was fed by debris flows and permafrost-related processes.

the Lamayuru Lake was an alpine lake in which the sedimentation was dominated by carbonate sedimentation, and that the carbonate-rich lacustrine deposits are typical of the northern Himalayan alpine lakes.

the Lamayuru Lake is a good model for the lacustrine stratas in the semi-arid environment of the Himalayan region and the lacustrine sediments of the Lamayurulake can be used as an example for other lacustrine sedi- mentation in the Himalayan region.
The main takeaway from our work is that
carbonate-rich alpine lakes can be important archives for the study of paleoclimate in the Himalayan region.

, in the Himalaya, the semi-arid alpine environment is conducive to the development of a diverse carbonate facies assemblage that is punctuated by occasional debris flows, whereas more humid conditions in the Himalaya south of the Greater Himalaya crest favor a more continuous clast-dominated sedimentation.
the Lamayuru lake is an excellent example of the type of lacustrine environment that would be common in the northern, alpine Himalaya.
